author: @musichicos
comment_text:
I’m writing from Argentina, and this video resonated with a phenomenon I frequently observe in local children: the repetition of decontextualized sounds from Japanese anime without any understanding of their semantic content. From a sociolinguistic perspective, “67” seems to function in a comparable way. Rather than operating as intentional slang, it behaves as a compulsive, low-threshold linguistic response shaped by digital overstimulation and by the social anxiety of not wanting to be excluded.

These sound fragments become indexical markers of group belonging. Their meaning lies not in the lexical content—often nonexistent—but in the pragmatic function they serve: signaling alignment with a peer group, demonstrating cultural awareness, and participating in a shared digital repertoire. The algorithmic environment intensifies this effect, reinforcing the repetition until it acquires a quasi-automatic, tic-like quality.

In that sense, “67” is indeed “brainrot,” but it also exemplifies a broader global trend: the emergence of meme-based micro-linguistic units that detach entirely from their origins and circulate as tools for affiliation, humor, and social cohesion. It’s fascinating to see how similar mechanisms arise across distinct cultural contexts.

Hence the “brrt” in “The way that switch brrt”.

author: @DrDanLawrence
comment_text: Great analysis. As a rhetorician, I'm interested in another set of questions about why this is a successful meme, regardless of its meaning. I think much of the success of this meme is in the construction of the phrase itself, and the way it is expressed (alliteration, inflection, its melody/musicality). I recently attended an event at the elementary school with my children, and, at least locally, here, the "6-7" is expressed with a particular rhythm and inflection. You have the alliteration of "six" and "seven," but also this kind of descending inflection which gives it a rhythm and melody, a general musicality. What makes a meme successful is its ability to replicate, and these elements of the phrase give "6-7" a kind of catchiness that is akin to the melody of a catchy song: a hook. The phrase makes itself want to be said again, which is what makes a successful meme--it has a kind of propulsion to hijack and replicate, it moves itself through populations almost as if against the will of the hosts. I agree generally with your analysis of the various meanings of the phrase, but think that you missed out on the part of the question that asks: "What is particular about this phrase that makes it spread rapidly?" or something in that ballpark. To just back up a bit, and to illustrate more generally what I'm talking about, we can observe infants babbling with rhythm and pitch that mimics adult language; infants and toddlers typically learn the rhythms and patterns of speech before they learn the meaning of words. And I think a similar phenomenon is occurring with a phrase like "6-7" which contributes to its replicability/memetic nature (as well as the in-group signification that you mention). In part, it is the phrase's meaninglessness which contributes to its success: like a musical melody, it is a relatively blank slate open to interpretation for different uses within different groups. There is also the sillyness factor (I'm thinking of the work of Huizinga in Homo Ludens and the nature of play behavior in humans--we are a silly species that plays games, and this "6-7" is a kind of expression of playfulness that is related to human learning and development and early childhood socialization).

comment_text:
My favourite language revival story:
Czech is spoken in the Czech Republic today thanks to a massive revitalisation effort in the late 1800s. At that point German was the official language in the Czech lands. Czech was mostly spoken in the countryside and by uneducated people because German nobles had most of the influence. Many Czech books were lost during that time and it was pushed out of higher education in favor of German. 
However, a large scale national identity movement was happening in Europe at the time and the Czechs were no exception. A group of Czech scholars collected the language, unified the grammar, wrote and distributed books, newspapers, founded theatres... All this was done with a focus on improving the general public's education level which helped to spread the language even more. It's noticeable to this day - although Czech did go through natural changes (mostly simplification of grammar), it's still very structured. If you ask "why is XY written like that?" it's nearly always because there's a clear rule for it. (Whereas with English I often have to look into the history/evolution of a word if I want to know more than "because it just is".)

video_title: Struggling to understand Gen Z Slang
author: @FlynnGorman
comment_text:
For those who needed a Gen Z translation, here you go:

finna: abbreviation of 'fixing to', meaning 'going to'.

glow-up: a mental, physical or emotional transformation (based on the change in appearance following a make-over) - in this case, used to mean 'an upgrade'.

high-key: as opposed to low-key, when something is the truth or to mean 'very much'.

sus: abbreviation of suspicious (originating from the game Among Us, where someone being sus meant they were likely the bad guy). Used to describe something as questionable, suspicious or poor quality.

literally: used to emphasise something that is figurative (not really the case/an exaggeration) or to mean that something truthfully is the case.

boomer: a person of the baby boomer generation, though commonly used to refer to anyone old or not gen Z.

lag: the slowing-down of a video game.

deadass: meaning 'seriously' or 'very much', originating from 'dead serious' (meaning you're not laughing and have a dead-pan facial expression because you're that serious).

cringe: when someone/something is embarrassing or awkward, making you feel embarrassed or ashamed.

Valorant: a free-to-play first-person hero shooter video game which is popular at the moment.

vibe: atmosphere/experience.

L: abbreviation of loss, meaning losing a round of a video game, or more generally doing poorly/a bad experience in life.

yeet: to throw something with great force (from the meme 'ya ya ya yeet').

cap: 'lies'. Commonly used in the phrase 'no cap' to mean that someone is telling the truth and is serious.

CEO of ___: meaning someone should be known for the following trait, as that is a good descriptor of them.

much: used at the end of a sentence to emphasise that something is very much the case. Originally used in sentences to ask if someone does something very often (e.g. 'do you go to the gym much?' could be shortened to 'gym much?).

whole-ass: describing something entirely or thoroughly.

snack: someone or something that looks good. Originally used to suggest that you'd like to 'taste' that person (sexual connotations).

OTP: abbreviation of 'one true pairing', meaning that something or someone is meant for you/is your soulmate.

dog-water: 'trash'. Used to describe something or someone as very bad (because dog-water from a used dog bowl would be very bad water to drink).

it's the ___ for me: referring to a feature of something/someone that stands out in a positive or negative way (originally used to emphasise the characteristic that someone loved about something/someone).

actual: once again affirming that what is being said is serious.

take several seats: when someone is doing too much or trying too hard (and is perhaps ineffective at this) so should sit down and be quiet so as not to make a fool of themselves.

cheugy-ass: cheugy means mocking someone as uncool (out of touch with the common slang of the current generation). '-ass' reiterates that this is a characteristic of the store.

cancel: to dismiss/reject someone/something publically, such that it becomes irrelevant due to current drama (which many people agree is unacceptable).

the planet you're responsible for killing: blaming the older generations for not doing anything to combat climate change, so that Gen Z has to fight to fix it.

setup: meaning your P.C. setup, including the keyboard, mouse, monitor(s), microphone, webcam, other accessories and P.C. itself.

bet: meaning 'sure', 'no problem', or 'I agree' or confirming that something is true. Originating from "you can bet on this".

'I got you': I understand you and/or can help you. 'Leave this with me'.

chill: describing something as cool and being something no one would have a problem with.

zaddy: describing something as sexually attractive. Originally describing a sexually attracting man (from the term 'sugar daddy' meaning someone who will provide you benefits or pay you for sex).

rig: a custom setup, such as a P.C. setup.

iconic: used to describe something in a very approving manner, suggesting that it could be influential or well-known or its quality.

drip: something that someone could attain which is cool and stylish. Originally referring to a cool or stylish outfit or to expensive jewellery.

slaps: describing something as excellent or amazing. Originally from the description of a song ("it slaps!") as something very groovy that someone would want to dance to (perhaps with the bass being slapped - that is - percussively slapping the string when playing a note for emphasis).

snatched: describing something as good looking, such that you'd want to grab it quickly before others could get to it.

stan: meaning you are obsessed with it and would go to great lengths for it (a mix of stalker and fan). Also credited as a reference to the Eminem song 'stan' about one of his overly-obsessed fans.

period: as in 'full stop'. Meaning that this is the end of the sentence/argument and nothing else needs to be said.

sweet: meaning something is awesome or nice.

hover some plastic: plastic is used to refer to a credit/debit card due to the plastic material it is made from. Hover some plastic refers to holding the card above the card reader using the microchip for its paywave technology. Basically, 'pay for it'.

'gucci': meaning something is awesome/cool/chill. Based on the expensive luxury fashion brand Gucci.

Hopefully that's helpful! Just try not to slip these unnaturally into your conversation with a Gen Z individual or it might be deadass cringe.

Here's what I learnt -

What is Brainrot? 
: It is the continuos stimulus that we provide to our brain which leads to alarmingly low attention spans, no deep work capacity and sky-high dopamile base levels.

What hints it is a brainrot?
: Even the single ping of notification from our phone leads to we wasting our next 2-3 hours on social media or worthless content, The inability to stick to what we plan to do even after knowing it, but can't manage to get the willpower to get up, and finally the losing of interest in everything that we do.

Well how to cure it?
: First and the most important thing- spend less time on your phone (ie. slacking off), then start spending time doing what really matters while being completely present in the present (yes), start spending more time with individuals (it might not sound much of an advice, but it is one for the people who spend their days in cave ..... Like me). And then for lowering the dopamine baselines- do nothing stimulus, or embrace the natural dopamines- eg. that we get from drawing, but without reference, without music, just pure flow of our childish creativity. 

For a finishing note: none of this phone thing and social acceptance seeking will matter 5 years from now, we have to think of it in long term and there're 2 things that I like to use as pedestal- 1. How our parents want us to turn out like and 2. How we want our children to feel when the look at us. Hope you all have an amazing life👍🏻

author: @luffirton
comment_text:
I think the biggest issue here is that there is no time limit on social media use for under 16’s
Why not restrict use to 45 minutes a day with parents being able to extend up to 3 hours a day.

Why not have time restrictions at night on weekdays to prevent children from being disturbed and distracted by social media and disrupt learning activities the next day.

Why not categorize children into age groups so 13-14 can use social media for 45 minutes a day and not between 21:00 and 06:30
15-16 year olds can use it for 1 hour and 45 minutes a day and not between 22:00 and 06:30

I ultimately believe the screen time might contribute even more to the negative impact social media can have. Screen time is too high and it prevents them from developing good healthy habits with social media. By limiting there use by time instead of just age we give young people the possibility to enjoy and participate in online learning, express themselves and activities while making sure these apps are accessible only for limited use and not when other activities is appropriate for them like sleeping.

You could argue that it parents responsibility to limit screen time and use of social media, but like the reporters stated it is a constant battle and it’s one that can’t be won if the teen wants to be on social media they then will find a way. So by actually limiting there availability by time would be a solution to experiment with than a blanket ban right away, if other measures don’t work then a blanket ban might after evaluation of the other measures would be necessary.

Age assurance technologies would be needed to ensure children are put into the right age category and that no children under 13s are are allowed or are holding accounts.

author: @stoicismwithtanner
comment_text: A young person's rational faculty is too easily manipulated and shaped toward vice. It's not because they're stupid -- they're not -- it's because they don't have enough information or experience to make an informed decision about the views they "take on board" as truth. Part of raising children is pacing their exposure to certain ideas and concepts, and CERTAINLY to ensure that the voices introducing those ideas and concepts are trusted and acting in good faith. 16 is a good age, the child should have a well enough constructed moral foundation at that point that they can confront the nonsense of the social internet. This isn't a a punishment, it's a responsibility we have as parents to raise our children and provide them with the tools they need to make better choices (and to be a bit more street smart) when they encounter the "real world." The Social internet is getting between parents and children, usurping the parents' efforts and moulding children too early and in a number of radicalized directions. It is, in a very real way, abuse to expose children to adult concepts, ideas, media, et cetera before a certain age. 16 is somewhat arbitrary but an age has to be chosen and that seems, on the average, like a good age. We don't like them drink before a certain age because the body needs time to be able to cope with alcohol (in as much as the body ever truly copes with alcohol), and the same is true of the mind... it has to be ready before it can be even moderately trusted to choose what is good for it.

author: @Aiphiae
comment_text:
I'm a high school teacher. The shift in how my students attend to coursework, lessons, conversations, and assignments over the last decade has been *profound.* It's shocking. I don't know a *single* teacher who hasn't commented on it. We have had to completely overhaul how we deliver information because the students can't focus. 

If I ask students to read a paragraph - a freaking *PARAGRAPH* - I will get numerous audible complaints about how hard it is to read and how boring it is. They don't even want to focus on a 5 to 8 sentence block of text. 

Of course, not *ALL* students are like this but the baseline has shifted so far in this direction that we've had to adjust for it. I hear it from colleagues in elementary, my co-workers in high schools, and even people I know who are profs in university.

Something has changed - whether it's "brain rot" media or just a lack of focus due to overstimulation from tech devices in general, I don't know. I do know, however, that my students today are *FAR* worse at the tasks my students 10, 15, or even 20 years ago would have found so *easy* they'd consider it *boring.*

comment_text:
VSauce's video titled 'Illusions of Time,' which was even before the rise of TikTok, has really stuck in my mind. Paraphrasing, the 'holiday paradox' about how you feel about time depends on whether your activity is empty or full: a four hour delay at the airport on the way to a vacation can feel unbearably long, but an exciting day on your vacation can feel really short. A week later, when recalling the memories retrospectively, the delay at the airport is a blip in your mind and the day of sightseeing feels like it was longer.  

Spoilers for the end of the video: there's also the 'TV paradox,' rapid stimulation experiences like scrolling are novel and exciting, they feel like they go fast, and yet when you recall them, they also feel like it went by fast, you barely remember anything. "You're burning time from both ends."

comment_text:
I think there is a major logical flaw in this video regarding the "cumulative effect" of brain rot.

I had hope when you mentioned the goldfish study—it's the perfect example of people latching on to some random study and spreading misinformation.

@9:30 The section on attention span relies on the "window switching" metric, which is a flawed proxy for focus. In 2004, we had single-window workflows (just Word). In 2020, we have multi-tab workflows. Switching windows every 40 seconds isn't necessarily a loss of focus; it’s often just modern multitasking.

Regarding the memory tests: They found that using TikTok taxes the brains short term memory more than resting. That isn't "brain rot," that is just cognitive load. If I run a mile and then try to sprint, I will be slower than if I had rested. That is fatigue, not permanent damage. That doesn't mean there are no degenerative effects, but you cannot just jump to the fallacy.

The real danger of Shorts isn't the format, it's the misinformation they spread.

author: @Keralite29
comment_text:
I really appreciate this video. 

Even though I'm easily able to ignore short-form content platforms altogether due to my disdain for the content almost always being both vapid in subject matter and hideous in its visual presentation, I nevertheless decided that I need to start confronting the mass social engineering that we're all being subject to and determine a path forward which involves complete abstinence from the modern outlets that I deem harmful to human health.

While this video explores the impact of social media on attention span, another area which I strongly believe it has impacted is our _vocabulary_ span. Studies have shown that the American vocabulary has significantly shrunk from its observed levels several decades prior. Reading for pleasure is at an all-time low relative to the 50s, a trend which began well before the advent of social media, but which social media has only exacerbated. Since social media has largely replaced reading as a downtime activity, it follows that most of the language exposure people face outside of the workplace comes from social media. The predominant mode of communication on social media is _slang_, rather than proper syntax. And if the majority of social media communication exists in slang, then this in turn hinders individuals from acquiring new vocabulary which is _not_ slang, which not only limits the range of concepts they can outwardly express, but more insidiously the range of concepts their minds actually _think_ in. 

Watch any street interview from the 1960s, in which individuals across various backgrounds (i.e white collar, blue collar) are surveyed, and you'll immediately observe just how staggeringly articulate these individuals are relative to us. 

I've rarely seen anybody else comment on this, whether on social media or elsewhere, but I'm confident this deterioration of language will have profound impacts on human intelligence, and what we can apply it towards.

I remember spending time in a library looking through card catalogs, early computerized search tool, and just following in-paper references, pulling books off shelves, looking through microfilm and microfiche, and spending hours after hours compiling sources to write one stinking high school paper. When Wikipedia came around, people were citing articles as a source in their papers. The argument of "anyone can put anything on Wikipedia, so you can't trust it" was all over the place. You can't just stop at the first layer and say "job done." It is truly terrifying that an AI slop article or video can suddenly become a source for another. Even when someone checks for references, they rarely carry that work back through until they find something like a paper published in a reputable journal that insists on peer review and publishes retractions when mistakes are later found. It's already a huge issue that people will justify saying nearly anything (including the President) by referencing something someone just made up from their own imagination. Checking and verifying sources can be hard work, but the internet currently barely enforces a standard of half-way looking one-deep without even the slightest bit of questioning the integrity of that one-deep source. It's terrifying.

author: @miriams.4341
comment_text:
I always struggle with these studies, because the phone is pretty much a tabular rasa. It is just what you make of it. To me saying “Don’t touch your phone” is on a similar level of helpfulness and practicality as “Don’t read any letters!” I would presumably also be less anxious and depressed if I stopped reading about all the bad things in the world every morning when I open the paper - would however make the next election kind of difficult, as I have no clue what is going on. 

Phones are here to stay and as a forgetful person in the countryside, NOT having one would actually be a complete catastrophe. My recipes are on my phone, my shopping lists, birthdays, appointments, a completely disproportionate audiobook library, hell - even my current knitting patterns. I know if there is a choir rehearsal tonight, because it is in a group chat. I can support a friend two countries over, despite being pretty busy, because the internet makes it financially justifiable. The problem isn’t with the phone, but how YOU have set YOUR tabular rasa up. You are constantly getting notifications? There are switches for that! I only get notifications for the important stuff and the rest will quietly coalesce into a list, until I’m ready to check it. 

To me, saying “just don’t use your phone!” is both impractical and shifting responsibility and while all or nothing thinking is attractive in its simplicity, it also usually doesn’t reflect reality. Moderation. Conscious choices when it comes to usage of time. Being honest with oneself. Those are the keys - not throwing a piece of tech across the room that only does exactly what YOU have set it up to do.

Just like the mouse addiction study, it wasn't that substances were that addictive as much as the rodents that had nothing else in their cage were more likely to be addicted to the substance, vs rodents that were in cages with other rodents and interesting toys to play with.

So it's not being on the phone for stretches at a time that CAUSES people to be more suicidal, as much as that they were on their phone that much because perhaps they hadn't found anything else in life that was rewarding enough to keep them off their phones. And THAT's more likely to be what increases suicidal feelings. 

Once again, correlation should not be confused with causation.

comment_text:
To add to this, it would benefit people to think of their brain as a muscle that must be trained like any other part of the body. If you don’t use it you lose it. 

Your brain does something called “synaptic pruning”. You can think of it like a spring cleaning for your neural pathways. If you are not exercising certain pathways, your body will no longer waste energy on maintaining these neural networks and prune them. It’s much harder (more energy intensive)  to develop new pathways than maintain old ones. 

You have to challenge yourself frequently, with difficult texts, issues that require critical thinking etc. Do not let yourself get caught idle in the day of endless information. Use it to your strengths. Push yourself. Be uncomfortable. Read hard books. Don’t use AI, learn how to research effectively on your own. How to analyze sources, biases, etc.

comment_text: Josephine, it is remarkable how close you get to Iain McGilchrist's hemisphere hypothesis without maybe being aware of it. I won't go into it here, but I very strongly recommend The Master and His Emissary, a book that I consider the very best I ever read because it transformed my life. (There's also no way I would have landed on your YouTube channel without having read it.) You brought up some Japanese thinkers, and I also see a Daoist thread moving through both Weil and Scovel Shinn. There are two Daoist concepts I really think fits Weil's approach to attention: namely "the uncarved block" and "wuwei." Essentially, in the West we view an unstarted project metaphorically as an empty canvas, while the East, an unstarted project is like an uncarved block. The uncarved block is unlimited potential, and so a work in progress is a release of this unlimited potential, towards a point where the potential is converted into actuality. A work is done when subtraction is no longer an addition. Wuwei is the idea of action through inaction, and this is quite different from doing nothing. It's possibly equivalent I think to what Weil means by detachment. It's not easy to do, and it requires effort to maintain, but detaching taps into that space that Scovel Shinn thinks of as superconscious mind. So as artists, we're moving from the potentiality of that uncarved block towards something more concrete, and we have to continually detach ourselves to get back into that superconscious mode along the way, so any thoughts of "productivity" is antithetical to beautiful art. And you can extend this block metaphor to other things involving a blank canvas, the main point is about being careful about getting stuck in that conscious mind mode, or that monkey mind mode, which is tragically linked to doomscrolling.

comment_text: One point you're sorely missing is IDLENESS. True idleness. The doomscrolling isn't just replacing your active time. It's more strongly sapping you of your idle time, of your time truly detached from activity. A human being in nature is not supplied with the means to be constantly productive, and neither is he meant to pursue constant productivity. The mind is meant to "waste time" (an absurd notion) because it is not unlimited in its power. Brainrot replaces the rest the mind needs with constant stimulation, which is stress just small enough to remain unfelt. I believe that's also an essential reason why you can't get anything done. You can't train if you're already stressed from what should be your rest. Imagine lifting heavy in the gym when you perpetually rep out light weights. You'll never be able to actually train hard. Conversely, your suggestion works because if you do train heavy enough you will be naturally forced to rest. You'll be so exhausted from proper intellectual activity that you will literally think about nothing in response. But it's important to realize that in our overstimulated world we should, at times— if not often— deliberately idle.

author: @kurczaczak
comment_text:
1. Short form often IS the correct form. Meetings that could be emails, emails that could be slack messages, slack messages that could be emoji reactions, meetings that could be emoji reactions. Quite often I see smart people blabbering and blabbering endlessly while the core ideas could be explained in a much more concise form. Good communication is concise communication, where you respect your audience by requiring no more and no less of their attention than strictly necessary.
2. I think that the internet brought a problem that is rarely discussed. When I was a child I'd have a pile of old magazines. There was nothing to do, so I'd read the same magazines over and over again, extracting every single bit of information from them. This is the way we can interact with information that allows us to form deeper thoughts and complex opinions. Nowadays though we have access to endless information, and even if someone carefully curates their feed to only consume meaningful information and carefully manages their attention, there's so much interesting stuff that the interaction "let me read this 100th time" doesn't happen again, which makes it nearly impossible to interact with media in ways other than surface-level.
3. I came to the conclusion that 100-hour RPG games are the S-tier form of artistic expression. Unfortunately, most AAA studios have undergone significant enshittification while indie studios don't have the budget to create such adventures, but these games are the only modern piece of media that allows interaction in the way I described. I am friends with some character not because I was told by the movie or the book "this character is friendly", but because I spent 10 hours of real life time across 10 weeks listening to their dialogues. I know the town well because I walked the same pathway literally hundreds of times. When there's a plot twist and some character betrays the protagonist, I personally feel betrayed even if I saw it coming BECAUSE I SPENT DAYS OF MY REAL LIFE TIME WITH HIM. Sure, it still isn't the same as "in the old days" because even if you complete the game, usually you turn it off, uninstall, and never return to it. But it's the closest we have.

I love the topic of the effect of technology usage. I saw it addressed multiple times in Dr.K. content. He is one of the biggest voices on the internet from the scientific community that raises worries about the topic. author: @edumazieri
comment_text:
Ok, to play devil's advocate a bit:
Is "focus" really always desirable? While it is true that some amount of focus is important for some topics and tasks, I don't think that more focus is always better. First, there are certainly diminishing returns: When first pondering over a tomato you might realize a lot of things about it relatively quickly, it's color, shape size etc., but then new realizations aren't going to come as quickly. So if you only ever focus on tomatoes, you're missing out on pondering over cucumbers and other fruits and vegetables, which could also potentially help you in better understanding the tomato.
That analogy was to illustrate my point that there is value to casting a wider net into the sea of knowledge  - and we're certainly doing this better than ever before. I grant that short-form content may be a bit too shallow for most topics, but I don't think that we're becoming less capable of focusing, I just think that since we got a much larger and varied buffet in front of us, we have the option of trying a little bit of everything before deciding what we like best.

One more point, regarding the part at 24:00. While certainly there are cases where seclusion happens, I feel like like the negative cases are amplified while the positive cases tend to be overlooked (possibly because they've become normalized, which is a good thing). For example, a lot of people, for one reason or another, can't or don't want to engage with people from their families, or schools and offices, and they would have spent their lives as social outcasts if not for the internet where they were able to find lots of people who share their interests and they can and want to meaningfully engage with. Getting bored in boring situations and seeking stimulation elsewhere might just be good sense.

I am also a victim of this brain rot. 2 months back my screen time was 11-13 hours + 8-10 hrs day sleep ( that was the worst time of my life, but I am happy that I have done a lot better now). But it definitely affected my brain a lot 
1.My attention span was so bad that I couldn’t read one paragraph without being distracted.
2. Second is memory loss, I started forgetting my life moments that were in my memory for years ( like my childhood fav memories, memories with friends, families)
3. I use to get irritated by small things.
4. I had no interest in literally anything, like there was nothing that could make me feel happy for even a short time.
5. I had a chill personality but now I get angry and irritated very easily.
6. Never had dark circles in my life but that month when my screen time was too much and I use to sleep in daytime, I got dark under eyes in just few days.
7.I felt so done and helpless with my life
8.My brain started slowing down, my brain’s processing speed was too slow.
9. No physical activity entire day.
And many more…🙂
It’s not like I never wanted to change this, I knew what I am doing is ruining my brain health and my future too but I just felt like a loser who can’t do anything because I felt so dumb and stupid that was the main reason my screen time got worst. I used my phone as an escape from reality. But one day I had enough, I gathered courage and decided to quit insta, tik tok etc and spend more time on my interests and outer world. I know I am still not doing good but it’s far better now. I hope I completely quit this addiction and rewire my brain for being productive.

comment_text:
I was kinda surprised that you (and the other references) didn't even touch on "unalive".  Arguably, it wasn't invented by Gen Alpha, but it really seems to have been embraced by them as slang in a way not done by any previous generation.  As far as I know, it was actually invented by Gen Z as a sort of tongue-in-cheek reaction to de-facto online censorship of words like "die", but for quite a long time was mostly used not as a general-purpose slang word, but very deliberately in specific situations to say "I am using this word because I am forced to, which is a commentary on the state of things".  Most Gen Zers wouldn't actually use "unalive" unironically in everyday conversations (which I think would be seen as a bit cringe to most of them).

However, a lot of Gen Alpha seems to have heard this word so much in Youtube videos, etc, that they have actually adopted it, entirely unironically, as a slang term which they use in their everyday lives.  What used to be a social/political statement is now just another word for the next generation.  So even if they didn't _invent_ the term, they have arguably invented _its use as ordinary slang,_ which I think is an interesting phenomenon in and of itself.

I'm the translator that used "sus" in an anime and upset so many people that it became trending on Twitter.
Some of the audience knew "sus" was a thing long before Among Us; others thought I was mistranslating it to try to look cool.
The word in Japanese was "kyodou fushin", which literally means to behave suspiciously, and the character says "kyodoru", which is the shortened (also somewhat old) slang version of the word.
It's been five years and I still get people harassing me about that completely unprovoked.

But also, it's interesting that a lot of the same words in different languages end up having equivalent slang words in other languages. Convergent evolution.

author: @cometsmith
comment_text:
chronically online person here with some added info:

12:48 if anyone really wants to know: the term skibidi comes from a song called Dom Dom Yes Yes, originally by Biser King and later became viral due to the cover by Fiki. The line "schtibidi dom dom yes yes" is (from my understanding) just scatting, and has literally no meaning. It became popular due to a Turkish man dancing along to it, where it stayed popular for a little while. After a while Alexey Gerasimo (a russian animator) made an animation of a video game character's head coming out of a toilet and singing the song, which went viral among Gen Alpha on scrolling apps like tik tok and youtube shorts. Gen Z and millennials found out about "Skibidi Toilet" (as it was affectionately titled) with basically no context (not that there was much to begin with) and found it hilarious because it seemed like the first piece of media that was made for Gen Alpha and not Gen Z, and made all of the 16-22 year olds feel old. From there people started ironically using the term "Skibidi" i think as just a nonesense word. Skibidi Toilet was so popular and it meant absolutely nothing that i think just mentioning it was humorous to the point where people would replace any adjective with skibidi for no reason, i.e, "Thats so skibidi" or "screw my skibidi life." It literally does not mean anything, to anyone, for any reason. 

18:40 while sheesh has been around for a long time, theres been a resurgence due to the "sheesh" memes. its old and dead by now but it was a meme where someone said sheesh in a funny high pitched voice and pointed to their arms (i think to point out the "ice in their veins"). So sheesh has been around for a long time, but it recently has a new reference that might add more context to the usage.

19:47 Similar to sheesh, sus has been around for a long time, but was rejuvenated with the Among Us craze during the covid pandemic. Among Us is a mafia-type game where there are imposters trying to kill other players, and since you were often typing or in heated debates, it was a lot easier to say sus rather than suspicious, and since so many people were saying it, I think its safe to say it regained popularity. It also has a double-meaning where people often use it to call someone gay? which im not sure if that was a common usage of it before Gen Z. Usually someone would call someone "sus" if they make a gay joke or do something somewhat gay, and not just as a straight up insult or slur.

20:03 I think it should be noted that I (as a member of Gen Z) have only usually ever heard this in sexual contexts, so maybe beware if you want to use this one in front of your kids or younger family. (someone correct me if im wrong here but i havent heard it used in many other contexts)

20:24 as far as im concerned, "yeet" came from a vine where someone threw something into a crowd and yelled "yeet!" If that isnt the origin of the phrase, it's definitely where it was popularized among Gen Z, as it went pretty viral. I distinctly remember a lot of people yelling yeet when they threw things in middle school.

What you said about people mistakenly thinking an old slang term is new reminds me of a conversation I had with a fellow Gen Xer in the 1990s at the University of Minnesota. Bear in mind that I grew up near Washington, D.C., and he grew up in rural Minnesota.

I described someone I didn't respect as a "schmuck." He replied, "I love that word! It's the perfect combination of 'shit' and 'fuck'!"

I was surprised to hear this and it turned out he thought it was a term recently invented by Gen X. I told him that it is a very old term and comes from Yiddish, not a portmanteau of Anglo-Saxon vulgarisms.

He said he thought it was new because he heard it from students who came "from big cities out east." I asked if those big cities were ones with large Jewish populations and he said, "Yeah, I guess they are."

I then asked if he'd heard professors using the word "schmuck" and he said he had, but he'd assumed they'd learned it from students.

I had to give him some credit, though. There's not much Yiddish spoken in rural Minnesota, so it's easy to understand that he hadn't heard "schmuck" until he got to the university. And to his credit, he correctly determined the meaning "contemptible person" from context clues. And although his hypothesis about the etymology was wrong, it was plausible.

author: @eritain
comment_text:
A fun thing to examine here is the "grunge speak" hoax. It was fake slang, but created by the processes that create real slang, for the same purpose as real slang.

Fake slang: It wasn't actually things widely said in the grunge subculture in 1992. 

Real slang processes: 

Megan Jaspers didn't like the band Tom Tom Club, so pretending their name meant "uncool outsiders" was that same representative-name thing as "Karen" and "Jeff." (And "Aiden." I saw what you did there, Dr Jones.) 

"Dish" for "attractive guy" was old-stock slang revived, and possibly given a gender flip (if it was previously used only for women, which I'm not sure of). 

"Bloated" for "drunk" was her deliberately playing with two interpretations of "had too much to drink." 

"Plats" for "platform shoes" was regular old clipping. 

"Bound-and-hagged" for "staying home on Friday or Saturday night" has so much going on, but among them, naming the effect after one of many possible causes is metonymy, and the cause itself is described with metaphor while playing with an existing idiom. 

The same purpose (broadly speaking) as real slang: making The Man feel left out, and making him look ridiculous when he tries to fit in. Which you know you're secretly hoping he's going to do. My generation loved watching boomers furrow their brow when we said something was "the bomb," but make no mistake, we also loved being horrified when they tried saying it themselves. 

(And now, having reached middle age [literally got called an old man for the first time last month!], I appreciate so much more how much the boomers enjoyed mis/using our slang and *watching* us be horrified.)

comment_text:
First off, excellent video. Gonna pass this around to my Boomer parents and Gen X co-workers, lost with all the rhetoric of the younger crowd. Even if I am a year behind, as of the date this video was posted. 

I thought "ick" or "what gives me the ick," was a shortened version of "icky," or "gross." Turns out, I was wrong. Similar, to "hawk tuah," (hock, being the appropriate word) it's the result of people trying to sound out a word, or in the case of "ick," an expression. The expression trying to be conveyed is one of annoyance, or "ugh." So, the "ick" is something someone does to annoy another, oftentimes unintentionally, or in some cases intentionally. In other words, a "pet peeve" or (when intentionally committed) someone being facetious.

Also, "Sigma" stems from the desire of all youth to find themselves, and be unique. In this case, they aren't or don't view themselves as vain and thus not the "main character" but they aren't a follower either (which they very much are with this line of thinking). So what's the next best thing? The mysterious lone wolf sigma. The "I don't care what other people think, I do my own thing" bad boy.

comment_text:
I just watched your video on "6-7". Great analysis. The best slang is local, regional slang.  I'm not sure why, but I seem to have a personal bias against using regional slang from other areas unless that slang is personally used with me. For me, as a millennial, and not being from Florida, I never started using "cap/no cap" and can't bring myself to say it to this day. From what I understand, it started as "capping on" someone, which meant to get over on someone, to trick to someone, to cheat someone, etc, and has since developed the now widely used truncated variants, "cap, that's cap, cap/no cap" etc. 

I remember in the late 90s and early 2000s when "twerk" and "treal" were in wide use, starting mainly with rappers in the south. I was a little disappointed years later to see the definition of twerk largely narrowed around the time when Miley Cyrus twerked in front of Will Smith's kids. 

I was very surprised at how "extra" made a comeback. We were saying that back in the 90s, but mostly as an adjective in the past tense I guess, or a verb with the preposition "out". "You extra'd, foo." "This muphucca over here hella extra'd out". Not like, "Becky, you are soooo eeeexxttraaa!". Or also as "having" extras, but with the verb "to get", but formulated in the past tense as being present (da fuq? I'm trying to make sense of it as I type (correct my grammar, please)). "This foo got hella extras." Or also coming with extras, as in , "This foo comin' wit da extras AGAIN? Gawddamn!"

"Woke", as became fashionable more recently, as far as I am aware, originally got its popularity from a rapper named Sno Tha Product. She used to call her brother early in the morning, who would help her film videos, book concerts, and whatever else was required for them to conduct their business for the day and ask him, "Is you woke? Is you woke yet?" Meaning, are you ready to grind? What are you waiting for, let's get to it!" She used the phrase a lot among her followers, had a good online presence and at the time, and even started a YT channel called "woke tv". From that, the phrase also began to be used in a pejorative sense by some of her followers. I.e. "You ain't woke.", meaning you don't have an understanding of what's going on, you're not as smart as I am, etc. From that point, I started hearing some younger, what would be described as left-learning activists, start to use the term in its pejorative sense to describe people who were misaligned with their values as "not woke". This was about 10 years or so ago. 

Thank you for all your content. I find it very interesting and refreshing!

comment_text: Skibidi goes way back. In my own family it was a shortened form of yippitee skippity, a lengthened form of yippee skippy. Then, once the 90’s rolled around I started hearing skater kids using it. I remember other groups of kids from other towns using it who seemed to have come up with it independently the same way. Then I met a girl from out of state who had named her cat skibidee. I also witnessed some kids at a punk show come up with it independently from bippity boppety boo. It was the late 80’s and early 90’s so no one had ever heard of the internet and none of us was bothering to write that stuff down. It’ll be forgotten and come back just like rawr! Rawr! was early 90’s twee slang but I also heard other kids pick up on it while still making a point that it was twee. Then I never heard it again until the emo scene kids happened.
